claim: Visual processing depends on specific computations implemented by complex neural circuits.
source: Visual processing depends on specific computations implemented by complex neural circuits.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract introducing the topic.

claim: An ON-Alpha ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs were described by a divisive interaction between excitation and delayed suppression.
source: We found that an ON-Alpha ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs were described by a divisive interaction between excitation and delayed suppression, which explained nonlinear processing that was already present in ganglion cell inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings and model fitting described in the manuscript.

claim: The divisive interaction between excitation and delayed suppression explained nonlinear processing already present in ganglion cell inputs.
source: We found that an ON-Alpha ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs were described by a divisive interaction between excitation and delayed suppression, which explained nonlinear processing that was already present in ganglion cell inputs.
evidence: This is supported by the DivS model performance on synaptic current data.

claim: Ganglion cell output was further shaped by spike generation mechanisms.
source: Ganglion cell output was further shaped by spike generation mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by the inclusion of spike-history terms in the full model.

claim: The full model accurately predicted spike responses with unprecedented millisecond precision.
source: The full model accurately predicted spike responses with unprecedented millisecond precision, and accurately described contrast adaptation of the spike train.
evidence: This is supported by model performance metrics showing >90% predictable variance captured.

claim: The full model accurately described contrast adaptation of the spike train.
source: The full model accurately predicted spike responses with unprecedented millisecond precision, and accurately described contrast adaptation of the spike train.
evidence: This is supported by the model's ability to predict responses at both high and low contrast with a single set of parameters.

claim: The retina contains ~30 distinct ganglion cell types.
source: Neural computations in the retina are generated by complex circuits that drive the responses of ~30 distinct ganglion cell types (Baden et al., 2016; Demb and Singer, 2015; Sanes and Masland, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many aspects of ganglion cell responses to visual stimuli can be predicted with a Linear-Nonlinear (LN) cascade model.
source: Despite the complexity of retinal circuitry, many aspects of the responses of ganglion cells to visual stimuli can be predicted with a straightforward Linear-Nonlinear (LN) cascade model (Shapley, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The LN model does not capture the effects of contrast adaptation.
source: However, many aspects of ganglion cell firing deviate from LN model predictions. For example, the LN model does not capture the effects of contrast adaptation, which includes a reduced gain (i.e., filter amplitude) at high contrast (Kim and Rieke, 2001; Meister and Berry, 1999; Shapley and Victor, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and demonstrated in the manuscript's data.

claim: Contrast adaptation includes a reduced gain at high contrast.
source: For example, the LN model does not capture the effects of contrast adaptation, which includes a reduced gain (i.e., filter amplitude) at high contrast (Kim and Rieke, 2001; Meister and Berry, 1999; Shapley and Victor, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The LN model does not predict firing at high temporal resolution.
source: The LN model also does not predict firing at high temporal resolution (Berry and Meister, 1998; Butts et al., 2016, 2007; Keat et al., 2001; Passaglia and Troy, 2004; Uzzell and Chichilnisky, 2004), and yet precise firing likely represents an essential element of downstream visual processing (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Havenith et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Precise firing likely represents an essential element of downstream visual processing.
source: The LN model also does not predict firing at high temporal resolution (Berry and Meister, 1998; Butts et al., 2016, 2007; Keat et al., 2001; Passaglia and Troy, 2004; Uzzell and Chichilnisky, 2004), and yet precise firing likely represents an essential element of downstream visual processing (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Havenith et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ON-Alpha ganglion cells comprise a major input to lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and superior colliculus.
source: We focused on ON-Alpha ganglion cells because they comprise a major input to lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and superior colliculus, and because they could be targeted routinely, in vitro, based on their large soma size.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ON-Alpha cells.

claim: ON-Alpha ganglion cells' spiking response to contrast modulation is mediated predominantly by synaptic excitation.
source: Furthermore, their spiking response to contrast modulation is mediated predominantly by synaptic excitation (Murphy and Rieke, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Spike responses were precisely timed from trial to trial at high contrast.
source: In high contrast, the stimulus evoked spike responses that were precisely timed from trial to trial (Figure 1A, left), consistent with previous work performed both in vitro and in vivo (Berry and Meister, 1998; Butts et al., 2016; Butts et al., 2007; Passaglia and Troy, 2004; Reinagel and Reid, 2000; Uzzell and Chichilnisky, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A and citations to previous work.

claim: Precision was not clearly present at low contrast.
source: Such precision was not clearly present at low contrast (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The LN model failed to predict either the SD of the first-spike in each event or the overall event duration in high contrast.
source: Based on this analysis, the LN model failed to predict either the SD of the first-spike in each event or the overall event duration in high contrast, but was largely successful in low contrast (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The LN model was largely successful in predicting spike timing properties at low contrast.
source: Based on this analysis, the LN model failed to predict either the SD of the first-spike in each event or the overall event duration in high contrast, but was largely successful in low contrast (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The LN+RP model could predict the temporal properties of the spike train at low contrast.
source: However, while the resulting LN+RP model could predict the temporal properties of the spike train at low contrast, it failed at high contrast (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The LN+RP model failed to predict temporal properties at high contrast.
source: However, while the resulting LN+RP model could predict the temporal properties of the spike train at low contrast, it failed at high contrast (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Spike-refractoriness alone could not explain the precision at high contrast.
source: Thus, spike-refractoriness alone could not explain the precision at high contrast, and consequently could not predict how the response changes from low to high contrast.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of the LN+RP model.

claim: Some degree of contrast adaptation is already present in a ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: Because some degree of contrast adaptation is already present in a ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs (Beaudoin et al., 2007; Beaudoin et al., 2008; Kim and Rieke, 2001), we hypothesized that we might uncover the source of the nonlinear processing by directly modeling the synaptic input currents.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At low contrast, the coherence of the excitatory current matched that of the LN model prediction.
source: At low contrast, the coherence of the excitatory current matched that of the LN model prediction, whereas at high contrast the coherence of the current extended to finer time scales (i.e., higher frequencies) and hence exceeded the precision predicted by the LN model (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At high contrast the coherence of the current extended to finer time scales and exceeded the precision predicted by the LN model.
source: At low contrast, the coherence of the excitatory current matched that of the LN model prediction, whereas at high contrast the coherence of the current extended to finer time scales (i.e., higher frequencies) and hence exceeded the precision predicted by the LN model (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The linear filter for the current responses had a larger amplitude in low contrast compared with high contrast.
source: The linear filter for the current responses had a larger amplitude (i.e., higher gain) in low contrast compared with high contrast (Beaudoin et al., 2007; Beaudoin et al., 2008; Kim and Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous work.

claim: Contrast adaptation occurred rapidly after the contrast switch.
source: This adaptation occurred rapidly after the contrast switch and showed a barely discernable slow component that has been observed in other ganglion cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; [Baccus and Meister, 2002; Manookin and Demb, 2006]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: The contrast gain was significantly larger for spikes (1.61 ± 0.23) than for currents (1.10 ± 0.14; p<10−6).
source: The contrast gain was significantly larger for spikes (1.61 ± 0.23) than for currents (1.10 ± 0.14; p<10−6, unpaired two-sample t-test, spikes: n = 11, current: n = 13) (Zaghloul et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measured data.

claim: Both contrast adaptation and temporal precision in ON-Alpha ganglion cell spike responses are generated in large part by retinal circuitry upstream of the ganglion cell.
source: These observations suggest that both contrast adaptation and temporal precision in ON-Alpha ganglion cell spike responses are generated in large part by retinal circuitry upstream of the ganglion cell, but that further transformation occurs between currents and spikes (Kim and Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of current and spike data.

claim: Further transformation occurs between currents and spikes.
source: These observations suggest that both contrast adaptation and temporal precision in ON-Alpha ganglion cell spike responses are generated in large part by retinal circuitry upstream of the ganglion cell, but that further transformation occurs between currents and spikes (Kim and Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in contrast gain between currents and spikes.

claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs to ganglion cells come from bipolar cells.
source: Excitatory synaptic inputs to ganglion cells come from bipolar cells, and bipolar cell voltage responses to our stimuli are well described by an LN model (Baccus and Meister, 2002; Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Bipolar cell voltage responses to our stimuli are well described by an LN model.
source: Excitatory synaptic inputs to ganglion cells come from bipolar cells, and bipolar cell voltage responses to our stimuli are well described by an LN model (Baccus and Meister, 2002; Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanisms responsible for the nonlinear behavior of the postsynaptic excitatory current are localized to the bipolar-ganglion cell synapses.
source: This suggests that mechanisms responsible for the nonlinear behavior of the postsynaptic excitatory current are localized to the bipolar-ganglion cell synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the LN behavior of bipolar cells.

claim: Possible sources of nonlinear behavior include presynaptic inhibition from amacrine cells.
source: Possible sources of such nonlinear behavior include presynaptic inhibition from amacrine cells, which can directly gate glutamate release from bipolar cell terminals (Eggers and Lukasiewicz, 2011; Euler et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2008; Zaghloul et al., 2007), and synaptic depression at bipolar terminals caused by vesicle depletion (Jarsky et al., 2011; Markram et al., 1998; Ozuysal and Baccus, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Possible sources of nonlinear behavior include synaptic depression at bipolar terminals caused by vesicle depletion.
source: Possible sources of such nonlinear behavior include presynaptic inhibition from amacrine cells, which can directly gate glutamate release from bipolar cell terminals (Eggers and Lukasiewicz, 2011; Euler et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2008; Zaghloul et al., 2007), and synaptic depression at bipolar terminals caused by vesicle depletion (Jarsky et al., 2011; Markram et al., 1998; Ozuysal and Baccus, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The suppressive filter was delayed relative to the excitatory filter (10.9 ± 2.2 ms, p<0.0005, n = 13).
source: For each cell, the suppressive filter was delayed relative to the excitatory filter (10.9 ± 2.2 ms, p<0.0005, n = 13, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The excitatory nonlinearity was approximately linear over the range of stimuli.
source: The excitatory nonlinearity was approximately linear over the range of stimuli (Figure 2D, left), whereas the suppressive nonlinearity decreased below one when the stimulus either matched or was opposite to the suppressive filter (Figure 2D, right), resulting in 'ON-OFF' selectivity to both light increments and decrements.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The suppressive nonlinearity decreased below one when the stimulus either matched or was opposite to the suppressive filter, resulting in 'ON-OFF' selectivity.
source: The excitatory nonlinearity was approximately linear over the range of stimuli (Figure 2D, left), whereas the suppressive nonlinearity decreased below one when the stimulus either matched or was opposite to the suppressive filter (Figure 2D, right), resulting in 'ON-OFF' selectivity to both light increments and decrements.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The DivS model outperformed the LN model in predicting the observed currents.
source: The DivS model outperformed the LN model in predicting the observed currents (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 2-D model did not perform significantly better than the DivS model.
source: While this 2-D model contains many more parameters than the DivS model, it did not perform significantly better (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The estimated 2-D nonlinearities for each neuron were well approximated by the separable mathematical form of the DivS model (R2 = 0.94 ± 0.02).
source: indeed, the estimated 2-D nonlinearities for each neuron were well approximated by the separable mathematical form of the DivS model (R2 for 2-D nonlinearity reconstruction = 0.94 ± 0.02; Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The AddS model had significantly worse predictive power than the DivS model (p<0.0005, n = 13).
source: The AddS model had significantly worse predictive power than the DivS model (p<0.0005, n = 13; Figure 2E)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The DivS model predicted the time course of the synaptic currents at low contrast using a single set of parameters.
source: Indeed, using a single set of parameters, the model was similarly accurate in both contrast conditions (Figure 3A), and outperformed an LN model that used separate filters fit to each contrast level (e.g., Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The DivS model outperformed an LN model that used separate filters fit to each contrast level.
source: Indeed, using a single set of parameters, the model was similarly accurate in both contrast conditions (Figure 3A), and outperformed an LN model that used separate filters fit to each contrast level (e.g., Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The DivS model implicitly adapts to contrast with no associated changes in parameters.
source: The DivS model thus implicitly adapts to contrast with no associated changes in parameters.
evidence: This is inferred from the model's performance across contrasts with fixed parameters.

claim: At low contrast, the DivS model becomes dominated by the excitatory term and closely matches the LN model.
source: At low contrast (Figure 3C, right), both excitatory and suppressive filter outputs are proportionately scaled down. Because the suppression is divisive and close to one, the DivS model becomes dominated by the excitatory term and closely matches the LN model, as well as the measured excitatory current.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and explained by the model structure.

claim: The changes in filtering properties predicted by the DivS model were tightly correlated with those from the measured data.
source: Indeed, using LN analysis to describe the DivS-model-predicted currents across contrast shows that the changes in filtering properties predicted by the DivS model were tightly correlated with those from the measured data (Figure 3D), including changes in contrast gain and biphasic index (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: A small tonic offset of the synaptic currents across contrast levels was captured by the DivS model without any parameter changes.
source: Furthermore, a small tonic offset of the synaptic currents across contrast levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which resulted in a vertical shift in the nonlinearity of the LN model (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was captured by the DivS model without any parameter changes (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The LNK model can predict the temporal features of ganglion cell intracellular recordings across contrast.
source: Indeed, a model of ganglion cells that explicitly implements synaptic depression, the linear-nonlinear-kinetic model (LNK model) (Ozuysal and Baccus, 2012) can also predict the temporal features of ganglion cell intracellular recordings across contrast.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The LNK model captured excitatory currents in response to the temporally modulated spot.
source: For our data, the LNK model captured excitatory currents in response to the temporally modulated spot (Figure 4A), also outperforming the LN model (p<0.0005, n = 13), although not with the level of performance as the DivS model (p<0.0005, n = 13).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with statistical comparisons.

claim: The LNK model outperformed the LN model (p<0.0005, n = 13) but not with the level of performance as the DivS model (p<0.0005, n = 13).
source: For our data, the LNK model captured excitatory currents in response to the temporally modulated spot (Figure 4A), also outperforming the LN model (p<0.0005, n = 13), although not with the level of performance as the DivS model (p<0.0005, n = 13).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The spatial LNK model had rate constants that minimized the time that the model dwelled in the inactivated state.
source: Consistent with this resemblance to the LN Model, the spatial LNK model had rate constants that minimized the time that the model dwelled in the inactivated state (i.e., was 'suppressed') (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The LNK model in the spot-annulus condition exhibited little performance improvement over the LN model (1.8% ± 1.3%, p=0.016, n = 7).
source: Correspondingly, the LNK model in the spot-annulus condition exhibited little performance improvement over the LN model (predictive power improvement 1.8% ± 1.3%, p=0.016, n = 7; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The DivS model significantly outperformed the LN model with an improvement of 8.6% ± 3.3% (p=0.016; n = 7).
source: By comparison, the DivS model significantly outperformed the LN model with an improvement of 8.6% ± 3.3% (p=0.016; n = 7), and was 6.7 ± 2.8% better than the LNK model (p=0.016; n = 7).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of model performance.

claim: The DivS model was 6.7 ± 2.8% better than the LNK model (p=0.016; n = 7).
source: By comparison, the DivS model significantly outperformed the LN model with an improvement of 8.6% ± 3.3% (p=0.016; n = 7), and was 6.7 ± 2.8% better than the LNK model (p=0.016; n = 7).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of model performance.

claim: The suppressive term of the DivS model showed a very distinct spatial profile relative to excitation, with a greater drive from the annulus region.
source: The suppressive term of the DivS model showed a very distinct spatial profile relative to excitation, with a greater drive from the annulus region, while excitation was mostly driven by the spot region (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Excitation was mostly driven by the spot region.
source: The suppressive term of the DivS model showed a very distinct spatial profile relative to excitation, with a greater drive from the annulus region, while excitation was mostly driven by the spot region (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: The peak latency for the suppressive filter was 129 ± 16 ms within the spot region compared to 120 ± 15 ms within the annulus region (faster by 9.7 ± 4.3 ms; p=0.0156, n = 7).
source: The suppressive filter processing the spot region was typically slower than the annulus filter: the peak latency for the suppressive filter was 129 ± 16 ms within the spot region compared to 120 ± 15 ms within the annulus region (faster by 9.7 ± 4.3 ms; p=0.0156, n = 7).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measured latencies.

claim: The strong suppression in the surround detected by the DivS model could not be explained by the LNK model.
source: The strong suppression in the surround detected by the DivS model could not be explained by the LNK model, which cannot flexibly fit an explicit suppressive filter.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure of the LNK model.

claim: Suppression in the LNK model arises from excitation, and thus the two components share the same spatial profile.
source: Indeed, suppression in the LNK model arises from excitation, and thus the two components share the same spatial profile (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: The resulting model successfully captured over 90% of the predictable variance in the firing rate for all neurons in the study (median = 91.5% ± 1.0%; n = 11).
source: The resulting model successfully captured over 90% of the predictable variance in the firing rate for all neurons in the study (Figure 5F, median = 91.5% ± 1.0%; n = 11), representing the best model performance reported in the literature for ganglion cell spike trains considered at millisecond resolution.
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The DivS model represents the best model performance reported in the literature for ganglion cell spike trains considered at millisecond resolution.
source: The resulting model successfully captured over 90% of the predictable variance in the firing rate for all neurons in the study (Figure 5F, median = 91.5% ± 1.0%; n = 11), representing the best model performance reported in the literature for ganglion cell spike trains considered at millisecond resolution.
evidence: This is a comparative claim based on the model performance.

claim: The standard LN model had a median predictive power of 62.8% ± 1.9% (n = 11).
source: By comparison, the standard LN model had a median predictive power of 62.8% ± 1.9% (n = 11); which modestly increased to 68.8% ± 1.9% upon inclusion of a spike-history term (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The LN model predictive power modestly increased to 68.8% ± 1.9% upon inclusion of a spike-history term.
source: By comparison, the standard LN model had a median predictive power of 62.8% ± 1.9% (n = 11); which modestly increased to 68.8% ± 1.9% upon inclusion of a spike-history term (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Ganglion cell spikes are strongly shaped by the nonlinear computations present at their synaptic input.
source: This suggests that ganglion cell spikes are strongly shaped by the nonlinear computations present at their synaptic input, and that the precise timing of ganglion cell spiking involves the interplay of divisive suppression with spike-generating mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the model performance and structure.

claim: The precise timing of ganglion cell spiking involves the interplay of divisive suppression with spike-generating mechanisms.
source: This suggests that ganglion cell spikes are strongly shaped by the nonlinear computations present at their synaptic input, and that the precise timing of ganglion cell spiking involves the interplay of divisive suppression with spike-generating mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the model performance and structure.

claim: The parameters of the divisive suppression components could not fit without including a spike-history term.
source: We found that the parameters of the divisive suppression components could not fit without including a spike-history term, suggesting that each component predicts complementary forms of suppression.
evidence: This is an observation from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Each component predicts complementary forms of suppression.
source: We found that the parameters of the divisive suppression components could not fit without including a spike-history term, suggesting that each component predicts complementary forms of suppression.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to fit the model without both components.

claim: Divisive suppression is necessary to predict the correct envelope of the firing rate.
source: By comparing the two models without DivS (LN and LN+RP) to those with DivS (DivS and DivS–RP), it is clear that divisive suppression is necessary to predict the correct envelope of the firing rate (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DivS had little impact in the low contrast condition.
source: Note, however, that DivS had little impact in the low contrast condition, which lacked fine-time-scale features of the spike response.
evidence: This is observed in the model comparisons.

claim: The spike-history term had little effect on the envelope of firing.
source: By comparison, the spike-history term had little effect on the envelope of firing (Figure 6A, bottom), and contributed little to the fine time scales in the ganglion cell spike train at high contrast (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The spike-history term had the largest effect on accurate predictions of event reliability.
source: Instead, the spike-history term had the largest effect on accurate predictions of event reliability, as reflected in the event Fano factor (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A two-stage computation with both divisive suppression and spike refractoriness is necessary to explain the detailed spike patterning on ON-Alpha ganglion cells.
source: We conclude that a two-stage computation present in the spike-DivS model, with both divisive suppression and spike refractoriness, is necessary to explain the detailed spike patterning on ON-Alpha ganglion cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the model comparisons.

claim: The DivS model outperformed LN models that were separately fit for each contrast level.
source: As with the performance of the models of excitatory current (Figure 3), the DivS model outperformed LN models that were separately fit for each contrast level (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The ability to correctly predict the effects of contrast adaptation depended on both the divisive suppression and spike-refractoriness of the spike-DivS model.
source: The ability to correctly predict the effects of contrast adaptation depended on both the divisive suppression and spike-refractoriness of the spike-DivS model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing models with and without these components.

claim: The DivS correctly predicted the magnitude of contrast gain change across the population.
source: Across the population, the DivS correctly predicted the magnitude of this change (Figure 7C, top), as well as the changes in biphasic index across contrasts (Figure 7C, bottom), and outperformed models with either the divisive suppression or spike-history terms missing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Spike refractoriness contributed to the stronger effects of contrast adaptation observed in spikes relative to synaptic inputs.
source: As expected, spike refractoriness imparted by the spike-history term contributed to the stronger effects of contrast adaptation observed in spikes relative to synaptic inputs (Beaudoin et al., 2007; Kim and Rieke, 2001, 2003; Rieke, 2001; Zaghloul et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous work.

claim: At high contrast, spikes concentrate into relatively smaller time windows, leading to a consistently timed effect of spike refractoriness.
source: Specifically, at high contrast, spikes concentrate into relatively smaller time windows, leading to a consistently timed effect of spike refractoriness (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Fast contrast adaptation depends on nonlinear mechanisms at two stages of processing within the retinal circuit.
source: Thus, fast contrast adaptation – and more generally the temporal shaping of ON-Alpha ganglion cell spike trains – depends on nonlinear mechanisms at two stages of processing within the retinal circuit.
evidence: This is concluded from the model analysis.

claim: Both aspects of nonlinear processing originate at the level of ganglion cell synaptic inputs, shaped by divisive suppression, and become amplified by spike-refractoriness.
source: Both aspects of nonlinear processing originate at the level of ganglion cell synaptic inputs, shaped by divisive suppression, and become amplified by spike-refractoriness to generate the array of nonlinear properties evident in the spike train output.
evidence: This is concluded from the model analysis.

claim: Precise timing was already present in the excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: Precise timing was already present in the excitatory synaptic inputs, and can be explained by divisive suppression, which likely depends on a combination of mechanisms: presynaptic inhibition of bipolar terminals from amacrine cells and synaptic depression at bipolar cell synapses.
evidence: This is supported by the current recordings and model analysis.

claim: Divisive suppression likely depends on a combination of presynaptic inhibition of bipolar terminals from amacrine cells and synaptic depression at bipolar cell synapses.
source: Precise timing was already present in the excitatory synaptic inputs, and can be explained by divisive suppression, which likely depends on a combination of mechanisms: presynaptic inhibition of bipolar terminals from amacrine cells and synaptic depression at bipolar cell synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the model structure and circuit knowledge.

claim: Temporal precision of spike responses has been observed in the retinal pathway with both noise stimuli and natural movies.
source: Temporal precision of spike responses has been observed in the retinal pathway with both noise stimuli (Berry et al., 1997; Reinagel and Reid, 2000) and natural movies (Butts et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Temporal precision plays an important role in downstream processing of information provided by ganglion cells.
source: Temporal precision also plays an important role in downstream processing of information provided by ganglion cells (Stanley et al., 2012; Usrey et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High temporal precision has already presented in the synaptic current inputs at high contrast.
source: By recording at two stages of the ganglion cell processing, we demonstrated that high temporal precision has already presented in the synaptic current inputs at high contrast, and temporal precision of both current inputs and spike outputs can be accurately explained by the DivS model.
evidence: This is supported by the current recordings and model analysis.

claim: The same suppression mechanism likely underlies high temporal precision of LGN responses.
source: The same suppression mechanism also likely underlies high temporal precision of LGN responses, which can be captured by a model with delayed suppression (Butts et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Precision of LGN responses is inherited from the retina and enhanced across the retinogeniculate synapse.
source: Indeed, recordings of both LGN neurons and their major ganglion cell inputs suggest that precision of LGN responses is inherited from the retina and enhanced across the retinogeniculate synapse (Butts et al., 2016; Carandini et al., 2007; Casti et al., 2008; Rathbun et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Temporal precision in the early visual system likely originates from nonlinear processing in the inputs to retinal ganglion cells.
source: Therefore, our results demonstrate that the temporal precision in the early visual system likely originates from nonlinear processing in the inputs to retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the current study and previous work.

claim: The full spiking-DivS model did not incorporate any form of direct synaptic inhibition onto the ON-Alpha cell.
source: Note that the full spiking-DivS model did not incorporate any form of direct synaptic inhibition onto the ON-Alpha cell, consistent with findings that the impact of such inhibition is relatively weak and that excitation dominates the spike response in the stimulus regime that we studied (Kuo et al., 2016; Murphy and Rieke, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the model structure supported by citations.

claim: The contribution of spike-history term to precision seems minor.
source: Our results show that the contribution of spike-history term to precision – as measured by the time scale of events and first-spike jitter – seems minor, consistent with earlier studies in the LGN (Butts et al., 2016; Butts et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous work.

claim: The spike-history term does play an important role in spike patterning within the event and the resulting neuronal reliability.
source: Nevertheless, the spike-history term does play an important role in spike patterning within the event (Pillow et al., 2005) and the resulting neuronal reliability (Berry and Meister, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous work.

claim: Contrast adaptation could be explained by divisive suppression, which takes a mathematical form similar to previously proposed gain control models.
source: Such adaptation could be explained by divisive suppression, which takes a mathematical form similar to previously proposed gain control models (Heeger, 1992; Shapley and Victor, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by the model structure and citations.

claim: The same divisive suppression mechanism may also explain nonlinear spatial summation properties of ganglion cells.
source: Moreover, the same divisive suppression mechanism may also explain nonlinear spatial summation properties of ganglion cells (Shapley and Victor, 1979), because suppression generally has broader spatial profiles than excitation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the model structure and citation.

claim: Contrast adaptation is amplified in the spike outputs mostly due to spike refractoriness and changes of temporal precision across contrast.
source: Contrast adaptation is amplified in the spike outputs mostly due to spike refractoriness and changes of temporal precision across contrast.
evidence: This is supported by the model analysis.

claim: At high contrast, the response had higher precision and occurred within shorter event windows.
source: At high contrast, the response had higher precision and occurred within shorter event windows (Butts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citation.

claim: The accumulated effect of spike refractoriness was stronger within each response event at high contrast.
source: As a result, the accumulated effect of spike refractoriness was stronger within each response event.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal structure of responses.

claim: Divisive suppression has been observed in the invertebrate olfactory system.
source: Divisive suppression has been observed in the invertebrate olfactory system (Olsen and Wilson, 2008), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Bonin et al., 2005), the primary visual cortex (Heeger, 1992), and higher visual areas such as area MT (Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Divisive suppression underlying synaptic inputs to ganglion cells cannot be attributed to fluctuations in membrane potential or shunting inhibition.
source: Divisive suppression underlying synaptic inputs to ganglion cells cannot be attributed to fluctuations in membrane potential or shunting inhibition since we recorded synaptic currents under voltage-clamp conditions that minimize inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental conditions.

claim: Synaptic depression will generally result in excitation and suppression that have the same spatial profiles.
source: Although synaptic depression could also explain fast transient responses and contrast adaptation (Ozuysal and Baccus, 2012), synaptic depression will generally result in excitation and suppression that have the same spatial profiles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2), whereas we show that excitation and suppression have distinct spatial profiles (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulations in supplementary figures.

claim: The divisive suppression in our model likely depends partly on presynaptic inhibition from amacrine cells.
source: Therefore, the divisive suppression in our model likely depends partly on presynaptic inhibition from amacrine cells, which can extend their suppressive influence laterally (Euler et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial profile of suppression and citations.

claim: Earlier studies had shown that contrast adaptation persisted in the presence of inhibitory receptor antagonists.
source: This was somewhat surprising, because earlier studies had shown that contrast adaptation persisted in the presence of inhibitory receptor antagonists, suggesting that adaptation depended primarily on mechanisms intrinsic to the bipolar cell (e.g., synaptic depression), independent of synaptic inhibition (Beaudoin et al., 2007; Brown and Masland, 2001; Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lateral inhibitory mechanisms also play a role in generating adaptation under conditions with inhibition intact.
source: Indeed, synaptic depression was likely the primary mechanism for adaptation in conditions with inhibition blocked, but the present results suggest that lateral inhibitory mechanisms also play a role in generating adaptation under conditions with inhibition intact, at least for some retinal circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the current results and previous work.

claim: The ON-Alpha cell receives a relatively high rate of tonic release from presynaptic type 6 bipolar cells.
source: However, the ON-Alpha cell receives a relatively high rate of tonic release from presynaptic type 6 bipolar cells (Borghuis et al., 2013; Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The average excitatory synaptic input would change less during contrast modulation compared to a ganglion cell that received a lower rate of glutamate release.
source: Consequently, the average excitatory synaptic input would change less during contrast modulation compared to a ganglion cell that received a lower rate of glutamate release.
evidence: This is inferred from the high tonic release rate.

claim: An inhibitory mechanism for contrast adaptation may play a relatively prominent role for retinal circuits driven by high rates of glutamate release.
source: An inhibitory mechanism for contrast adaptation thus may play a relatively prominent role for retinal circuits, such as the ON-Alpha cell, driven by high rates of glutamate release.
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of ON-Alpha cells.

claim: Each ganglion cell type receives inputs from a unique combination of bipolar and amacrine cell types, contributing to a unique visual computation.
source: Detailed anatomical studies suggest that each ganglion cell type receives inputs from a unique combination of bipolar and amacrine cell types, contributing to a unique visual computation (Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Other ganglion cell types will perform different computations and have different roles in visual processing.
source: We expect that other ganglion cell types will perform different computations, and likewise have different roles in visual processing.
evidence: This is speculated based on the diversity of ganglion cell types.
